Assistant A's code is correct and meets both stated constraints. It runs in O(log(min(n, m))) time, which is within the requested O(n) bound, and uses O(1) extra space. Its opening claim that the request is "not possible" is wrong, though. An O(n) requirement is an upper bound, and a faster algorithm satisfies it. The code also has a minor edge-case issue: when both arrays are empty it returns infinity instead of raising an error.

Assistant B's recursive `findKth` is logically correct. It takes the literal O(n) time bound, but it violates the O(1) space requirement. Each recursive call uses slicing (`nums1[i:]`, `nums2[j:]`), which copies arrays and allocates O(n) memory in total. Its claim of "O(1) space since we do not use any extra space" is therefore false. Its time analysis is also loose because of the copying.

Assistant A delivers a correct, asymptotically better solution that satisfies both constraints, despite misstating the impossibility. Assistant B follows the requested bounds on paper but breaks the space constraint and misreports it. A is the better answer.

[[A]]
